stem: A 24-year-old man presents with fever, drooling, muffled voice, bilateral submandibular swelling, and elevation of the tongue after a dental infection. He has stridor and respiratory distress. What is the most important immediate step in management?
stemHtml: A 24-year-old man presents with fever, drooling, muffled voice, bilateral submandibular swelling, and elevation of the tongue after a dental infection. He has stridor and respiratory distress. What is the most important immediate step in management? (Question Id: 506047)
keywords: Bilateral submandibular swelling + elevation of tongue → Classic for Ludwig angina (rapidly spreading cellulitis of submandibular space).
Drooling + muffled voice + stridor → Indicates impending upper airway obstruction.
Dental infection with respiratory distress → Deep neck space infection causing airway emergency, requiring immediate airway control.
keywordsHtml:
1. Bilateral submandibular swelling + elevation of tongue → Classic for Ludwig angina (rapidly spreading cellulitis of submandibular space).
  2. Drooling + muffled voice + stridor → Indicates impending upper airway obstruction.
  3. Dental infection with respiratory distress → Deep neck space infection causing airway emergency, requiring immediate airway control.

C.title: Secure the airway
C.body:
Ludwig angina is a rapidly progressive cellulitis of the submandibular and sublingual spaces, usually arising from an odontogenic infection. Progressive edema elevates the tongue and compresses the airway. Patients commonly present with fever, drooling, muffled “hot potato” voice, dysphagia, and respiratory distress. Stridor is a late and dangerous sign indicating critical airway narrowing.
This patient already has stridor and respiratory distress, making airway compromise the most immediate life-threatening problem. Therefore, the first priority is securing the airway, often with awake fiberoptic intubation or surgical airway if intubation is difficult. Definitive treatment such as IV antibiotics and imaging comes only after airway stabilization.
C.bodyHtml:
Ludwig angina is a rapidly progressive cellulitis of the submandibular and sublingual spaces, usually arising from an odontogenic infection. Progressive edema elevates the tongue and compresses the airway. Patients commonly present with fever, drooling, muffled “hot potato” voice, dysphagia, and respiratory distress. Stridor is a late and dangerous sign indicating critical airway narrowing.

This patient already has stridor and respiratory distress, making airway compromise the most immediate life-threatening problem. Therefore, the first priority is securing the airway, often with awake fiberoptic intubation or surgical airway if intubation is difficult. Definitive treatment such as IV antibiotics and imaging comes only after airway stabilization.
C.clinicalReasoning: Airway obstruction is the leading cause of death in Ludwig angina. Presence of stridor indicates impending complete obstruction. ABC stabilization takes priority over all investigations and medications. Therefore, airway protection is the immediate life-saving intervention.

A.title: IV antibiotics
A.body: Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics are essential in Ludwig angina because the infection is polymicrobial, commonly involving streptococci and anaerobes from oral flora. Antibiotics help control the infection and prevent spread into deeper neck spaces or mediastinum.
A.bodyHtml: Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics are essential in Ludwig angina because the infection is polymicrobial, commonly involving streptococci and anaerobes from oral flora. Antibiotics help control the infection and prevent spread into deeper neck spaces or mediastinum.
A.clinicalReasoning: Although IV antibiotics are necessary, they are not the first immediate step in a patient with airway compromise. In a patient with stridor and respiratory distress, airway management always precedes antimicrobial therapy.
A.clinicalReasoningHtml: Although IV antibiotics are necessary, they are not the first immediate step in a patient with airway compromise. In a patient with stridor and respiratory distress, airway management always precedes antimicrobial therapy.

B.title: CT scan neck
B.body: CT neck with contrast helps evaluate the extent of deep neck space infection, abscess formation, and spread into adjacent fascial planes. It is useful after stabilization for diagnosis and surgical planning.
B.bodyHtml: CT neck with contrast helps evaluate the extent of deep neck space infection, abscess formation, and spread into adjacent fascial planes. It is useful after stabilization for diagnosis and surgical planning.
B.clinicalReasoning: Imaging should not delay emergency airway management. A patient with active respiratory distress may deteriorate rapidly while waiting for CT. Therefore, CT is performed only after the airway is secured.
B.clinicalReasoningHtml: Imaging should not delay emergency airway management. A patient with active respiratory distress may deteriorate rapidly while waiting for CT. Therefore, CT is performed only after the airway is secured.

D.title: Oral corticosteroids
D.body: Corticosteroids may reduce inflammatory edema and can sometimes be used as adjunctive therapy in airway inflammation. They are not definitive therapy for deep neck infections.
D.bodyHtml: Corticosteroids may reduce inflammatory edema and can sometimes be used as adjunctive therapy in airway inflammation. They are not definitive therapy for deep neck infections.
D.clinicalReasoning: Steroids alone do not treat the infection or secure the airway. Oral steroids are especially inappropriate in a patient with severe airway compromise and inability to swallow safely.
D.clinicalReasoningHtml: Steroids alone do not treat the infection or secure the airway. Oral steroids are especially inappropriate in a patient with severe airway compromise and inability to swallow safely.

E.title: Observe overnight
E.body: Observation may be appropriate for stable mild infections without airway compromise. Ludwig angina, however, is an aggressive and rapidly progressive emergency.
E.bodyHtml: Observation may be appropriate for stable mild infections without airway compromise. Ludwig angina, however, is an aggressive and rapidly progressive emergency.
E.clinicalReasoning: This patient already has stridor and respiratory distress, indicating impending airway collapse. Observation would dangerously delay life-saving treatment.
E.clinicalReasoningHtml: This patient already has stridor and respiratory distress, indicating impending airway collapse. Observation would dangerously delay life-saving treatment.

keyConcept: Ludwig angina is a deep neck space cellulitis usually caused by dental infection. The most feared complication is rapid airway obstruction due to tongue elevation and soft tissue edema. In any patient with stridor, drooling, and respiratory distress, airway stabilization is the first priority before imaging or antibiotics.

The most feared complication is rapid airway obstruction due to tongue elevation and soft tissue edema. diagrams.description: This diagram illustrates Ludwig angina, a rapidly progressive cellulitis involving the submandibular, sublingual, and submental spaces, most commonly caused by odontogenic infection. The image highlights the characteristic bilateral submandibular swelling, tongue elevation, and airway compression leading to stridor and respiratory distress. It emphasizes the emergency principle that airway stabilization is the first and most critical step before imaging or antibiotic therapy. The diagram also demonstrates pathophysiology, clinical features, airway management techniques, investigations, treatment strategies, and potential life-threatening complications.
